The post Liquid AI Releases d1-ultra: A Multimodal Decision Model That Scores 65 on the AA Decision Index appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Liquid AI has released d1-ultra , its most capable decision model to date. The Liquid AI d1-ultra decision model reads text, images, or both. It answers typed questions with a probability for each possible answer. It does this in one forward pass and generates no output tokens. For developers, that means classification, routing and scoring calls without paying for generated text. It is available now on the Liquid API at $0.042 per million input tokens. TL;DR Size: Parameters and context length not disclosed. Built on a larger open-weight backbone than d1. Runs on: Hosted Liquid API only. No downloadable weights or quantized variants announced. Performance: Leads all 8 categories in Liquid’s 112-evaluation suite, per Liquid. Best: 65 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, ranked #1 (Liquid-reported). Worst: No public per-benchmark breakdown or parameter count yet; claims are vendor-reported. What is a decision model? A decision model answers bounded questions with probabilities instead of free text. Liquid’s decision model docs describe 3 question types: Noul: a yes/no question that returns a probability between 0 and 1. Choice: one label from a set, with a probability per label. Score: a probability-weighted position on an ordered rubric. The docs recommend decision models for routing, moderation, guardrails, triage and LLM-as-judge replacement. They recommend a language model for summarization, chat and code generation. How does d1-ultra work? Each request carries a state (the context), optional images , and 1 or more typed questions . The model evaluates every question against the same input in 1 call. The d1 API reference shows responses with output_tokens always at 0. Liquid AI team states that d1-ultra uses a larger open-weight backbone than d1 , along with heavy Liquid-specific customizations. Combined with Liquid’s decision training pipeline, the gains are largest on knowledge tasks. Liquid AI team built d1-ultra for messy cases. Its examples include spotting a circuit board defect against a spec. Another is checking a damage claim against the customer’s photo. How does d1-ultra perform on benchmarks? Liquid AI compared d1-ultra against its earlier d1 and TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 across 112 evaluations. According to Liquid AI’s announcement , d1-ultra outperforms Jev 1.14 across all tasks at the same price. On the independent Artificial Analysis Decision Index , Liquid reports d1-ultra ranks #1 with a score of 65. The index averages 4 evaluations at 25% each: AA-Omniscience-Decision: knowledge and hallucination HLE-MultiChoice: reasoning When2Call: tool calling WildGuardTest: safety classification For context, Artificial Analysis’s Oct 13 launch article listed Jev 1.13 first at 58. GLiDE and Microsoft-Decision-1 followed at 54 each. Comparison: d1-ultra vs other decision models Feature d1-ultra d1 Jev (TypeSafe) Microsoft-Decision-1 GLiDE (Fastino) Developer Liquid AI Liquid AI TypeSafe AI Microsoft Fastino Labs Parameters Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Input Text, images Text, images Text Not disclosed Not disclosed Weights API only API only Closed Not disclosed Not disclosed AA Decision Index 65 (Liquid-reported) Not disclosed 58 (v1.13, Oct 13) 54 (Oct 13) 54 (Oct 13) Price $0.042 / 1M input Not disclosed $0.042 / 1M input $31 / 1M tasks (AA) $119 / 1M tasks (AA) Output tokens billed No No No Not disclosed Not disclosed How do you deploy d1-ultra, and what does it cost? d1-ultra runs on the Liquid API through the /decisions/v1/systemone endpoint with "model": "d1-ultra" . Liquid says Vercel AI Gateway and OpenRouter support is coming soon. You can test it first in the d1 Playground . Billing covers input tokens only. Per Liquid’s pricing notes , images cost 1.5 tokens per 32×32-pixel patch. A 1024×1024 image therefore costs 1,536 tokens. Each question is billed as its own prompt, including its text and all images. So 3 questions on 1 image bill that image 3 times. The endpoint docs cap requests at 8 images and 10,000 image patches. The full JSON body must stay under 4.5 MB. Key Takeaways d1-ultra returns probabilities for text and image decisions with 0 output tokens. Liquid reports a #1 score of 65 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index. It costs $0.042 per 1M input tokens, the same rate as TypeSafe’s Jev. Liquid claims the lowest calibration error in its tests, useful for routing thresholds. Size, backbone and weights remain undisclosed; access is API-only. Check out the official blog post , the decision model docs , and try the d1 Playground . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. The Perplexity SPACE sandbox gives each agent task its own Firecracker microVM. Credentials and outbound traffic are controlled from outside that VM. The code ships under Apache 2.0 on GitHub. For teams building coding or browsing agents, this is a production-tested isolation […] The post Perplexity Open-Sources SPACE, a Firecracker MicroVM Sandbox for AI Agents appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Perplexity has open-sourced SPACE , the sandbox platform behind every task in Perplexity Computer. The Perplexity SPACE sandbox gives each agent task its own Firecracker microVM. Credentials and outbound traffic are controlled from outside that VM. The code ships under Apache 2.0 on GitHub . For teams building coding or browsing agents, this is a production-tested isolation layer they can self-host. TL;DR Size: Rust codebase, release 0.8.0 , the public baseline. HTTP API plus server-sent events. Runs on: A Linux x86_64 host with KVM , /dev/kvm , btrfs and Docker. Local Kind (Kubernetes) or direct mode. No macOS. Performance: In production, median create latency fell from 185 ms to 60 ms versus Perplexity’s previous provider. Best: 0 of 108 VM-to-host escape attempts succeeded across 9 frontier models. Worst: Before fixes, agents bypassed the egress policy in 11 of 54 partial-network runs. What is Perplexity SPACE? SPACE (Sandboxed Platform for Agentic Code Execution) is Perplexity’s platform for running agent code in isolated microVMs. Applications call its HTTP API to create Linux environments, run commands and stream output. A template supplies the starting filesystem. A sandbox is one instance of that template, with its own VM and writable disk. Many commands can run inside one sandbox. Perplexity’s launch thread explains the design goal. Agents run commands, install packages and call services with root inside the sandbox. The host stays outside the guest’s control. Agent work is long-running, stateful and branching, so it must survive restarts. How does SPACE isolate agents? Each sandbox is a Firecracker microVM with its own guest kernel. A per-sandbox network gateway on the host enforces egress policy on every outbound connection. Secrets never enter the guest. Per Perplexity’s July engineering post , credentials are injected at the network layer. The credential store adds hierarchical scoping, rate limits and audit logging. The architecture guide splits the system into 4 parts. These are a PostgreSQL-backed API, controllers, worker services and a data plane. Worker services manage VMs, networking, volumes, templates and credentials. btrfs copy-on-write creates each root filesystem. How do pause, suspend and restore work? Sandboxes move through 4 states: running, paused, suspended and deleted. Paused: VM memory stays resident on the worker. This is not a durable snapshot. Suspended: VM memory, runtime state and root filesystem are snapshotted. Active resources are released. Idle default: sandboxes suspend after 6 hours without activity. For fast creates, Kubernetes deployments use warm pools of booted sandboxes. Single-node setups use base snapshots instead. In production, the 90th-percentile create latency dropped from 447 ms to 89 ms . Perplexity reports that 100% of Computer sessions run on SPACE. Did SPACE survive a red-team test? Perplexity’s Escaping SPACE: Part I report tested 9 models with root inside the guest. The study ran 216 runs across 2 tasks and 4 settings. Sandbox escape: 0 of 108 runs reached the host-side secret. No-network bypass: 0 of 54 runs succeeded. Partial-network bypass: 11 of 54 runs succeeded before fixes. 4 models found a path. Claude Opus 5.0, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Cyber and Kimi K3 found bypasses. The attacks used DNS spoofing and shared CDN IP addresses. Perplexity then added source-address validation through nftables. The gateway now terminates TLS and checks both SNI and HTTP host against the allowlist. In the retest, no model produced a verified bypass. The same team tested 10 third-party platforms. 8 showed at least one network-policy bypass. Perplexity disclosed the results to every affected vendor. oldContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 Sanctuary Computer: Head of Technology Anywhere in the World New York Full-Stack Programming Full-Time <img src="https://we-work-remotely.imgix.net/logos/0171/3386/logo.gif?ixlib=rails-4.0.0&w=50&h=50&dpr=2&fit=fill&auto=compress" /> <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> New York City <br /><strong>URL:</strong> <a href="https://sanctuary.computer">https://sanctuary.computer</a> </p> <p>We are hiring a <strong>Head of Technology</strong> for the garden3d creative collective, to lead engineering at Sanctuary Computer and garden3d in the era of agentic computer code.</p> <p><a href="https://garden3d.notion.site/Head-of-Technology-3f9131fea2c7815da5e3ec914835c397?source=copy_link"><strong>Original job posting link</strong></a></p> <h3><strong>About <a href="https://garden3d.net/">garden3d</a></strong></h3> <p>We are worker owned creative collective, innovating on everything from brands and IRL communities to IoT devices and cross platform apps. We share profit, open source everything, spin out new businesses, and invest in exciting ideas through financial and/or in-kind contributions.</p> <p>Our client roster includes Google, Stripe, Figma, Hinge, Black Socialists in America, ACLU, Pratt, Parsons, Mozilla, The Nobel Prize, MIT, Gnosis, Etsy &amp; Gagosian.</p> <p>We’re the software team behind innovative products like The Light Phone &amp; Mill, and we operate a global, decentralized community space collective called Index Space.</p> <p>We think of our garden3d as collective for creative people, prioritizing a happy, talented, and diverse studio culture. We work on projects that bring value to our world, and we balance deep care for the work we do with a genuine curiosity about life outside of our jobs.</p> <h3><strong>Sanctuary Computer - Development</strong></h3> <p>At <strong><a href="https://www.sanctuary.computer/">Sanctuary Computer</a></strong> we’re building a different type of technology shop – one that prioritizes close collaboration between the client and the craftsperson.</p> <p>Our projects range from design-forward websites, to robust web apps, to native mobile development.</p> <h3><strong>XXIX - Design</strong></h3> <p>When we started <strong><a href="https://www.xxix.co/">XXIX</a></strong> in 2013, we set out to create a different kind of design studio and we’ve thrived because we continually ask what a creative practice can be.</p> <p>We’re building a radically different kind of organization that values autonomy, growth, transparency, and shared responsibility.</p> <h3><strong>Index - Community</strong></h3> <p><strong><a href="https://www.index-space.org/">Index</a></strong> is network of physical spaces all around the world, Index provides space for the exchange of knowledge and tools.</p> <p>We nurture trust within the creative community through generosity and abundance of ideas and care.</p> <h3><strong><a href="https://feed.garden3d.net/">garden3d TK</a> — Media</strong></h3> <p>At garden3d, we’re in the early stages of building an experimental media company exploring emerging themes related to the evolving landscape of technology, design and culture.</p> <p>We aim to monetize this outlet, publish books, produce screenplays, and release music.</p> <p>Plus, our partner organizations</p> <p><strong><a href="https://www.thelightphone.com/">Lightphone</a><br></strong><strong><a href="https://www.mill.com/">Mill</a><br></strong><strong><a href="https://ingredient-ai.com/">IngredientAI</a></strong></p> <h2>⛰️ The Head of Technology Role</h2> <p>The garden3d Head of Technology has one mandate: everything we build works, holds up in production, and gets built the smartest way available to us. We are a house of brands - Sanctuary Computer (development), XXIX (design), Index Space (community), USB Club (digital community), and the garden3d umbrella itself - and a lot of what all of them ship runs on software we wrote. Working in close partnership with our founder &amp; president Hugh Francis, this person sets the engineering standard, and builds the culture that holds it.</p> <p>You can be based anywhere. A lot of our people are in New York and there's some gravity here, but we already work across timezones and we would happily hire in Europe, Singapore, Chicago, or wherever you are. If you're the right person, we want to hear from you.</p> <p>This role works with studio leads, developers, designers, project managers and clients across every garden3d vertical.</p> <p>This person can move between a Rails migration, a Next.js app, a firmware release plan and an agent loop in the same week, and raise the bar on each of them.</p> <p>They span all of garden3d, but their home base is Sanctuary Computer, where roughly 70% of their time goes. Our development studio is where the engineering standard gets set, and where it either holds or slips: architecture, code review, estimation, and the hardest technical calls on our biggest projects. The other 30% goes to garden3d's broader technology story: how we ship product for USB Club, build with agents across the collective, which tools and platforms we bet on, and what we build for ourselves.</p> <p>They are also how we get better people. Our work is only as good as the engineers making it, so this person hunts for exceptional talent, sells them on us, and sets them up to do the best work of their careers. The ideal candidate looks at a worker-owned collective with four studios, an open P&amp;L and clients like Google, Stripe, Brooklyn Museum and The Nobel Prize, and sees an engineering practice they can propel among the best in the world.</p> <h2><strong>Responsibilities &amp; Mandates</strong></h2> <h3>️ <strong>Systems that hold up</strong></h3> <p>We build web apps, native apps, data pipelines, content platforms and connected devices for clients who can't afford for them to fall over. This person has engineered complex systems for a long time, and it shows in the architecture they draw before a line is written. They own the technical blueprint on our most important projects, and they make the hard calls on the rest: what to build, what to buy, and what to leave out.</p> <h3> <strong>All in on agentic development</strong></h3> <p>The way software gets built changed, and we intend to be ahead of it. This person is already deep in it: loop engineering, agents running against evals, agents that open their own PRs, and the guardrails that make all of that trustworthy. They make agentic development the default way Sanctuary Computer works, and they can tell the difference between a demo and a system a team can rely on.</p> <h3> <strong>Practical engineering</strong></h3> <p>We strongly prefer convention over configuration, boring technology, and platforms that let a small team ship a lot. TypeScript is the default language, Rails and Phoenix handle what they're best at, and we'd rather deploy to a platform like Render or Heroku than run our own infrastructure. newContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 Legion: Principal Product Manager, Agentic AI Anywhere in the World 🇺🇸 United States of America Product Full-Time <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Remote, United States </p> <h1><strong>Principal Product Manager, Agentic AI</strong></h1> <h2>REMOTE, United States</h2> <p><strong>JOB OVERVIEW</strong></p> <p>Legion is building AI agents that carry out workforce management work, not agents that describe it.</p> <p>Much of what is presented as AI in workforce management today is a conversational layer over an existing scheduling screen. The more substantial problem — software that reasons over demand, labor regulation, and employee preferences, then acts, with a person in the loop wherever the stakes require one — remains unsolved across the category. Legion intends to solve it, and this role leads the product work to get there.</p> <p>You will take an agent surface from operational research through specification, prototype, evaluation, and enterprise deployment, working hands-on throughout. You will work closely with Legion's AI Lab engineers and with our CEO, who is engaged in this work daily.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>RESPONSIBILITIES AND DUTIES</strong></p> <p><strong>Agent definition.</strong> Determine what an agent is responsible for, which tools it may call, what it must escalate, what it must never do, and what a manager sees when it acts. These decisions affect employee pay and legal compliance. Much of this work is pre-launch, so you will shape the direction rather than inherit it.&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Problem selection.</strong> The hardest judgment in agentic product work is identifying which workflows suit an agent and which do not. You will spend substantial time inside customer operations — district managers, store managers, labor operations, frontline employees — and return with a ranked, defensible view of where an agent creates measurable value and where it does not.</p> <p><strong>The human-in-the-loop contract.</strong> Scheduling decisions affect income, childcare arrangements, and legal protections. For each agent action you will define where autonomy is appropriate, the escalation thresholds, how a manager overrides the system, what is logged, and how a compliance team audits the outcome. Legion treats this as a first-class design problem.</p> <p><strong>Build quality.</strong> You are accountable for what ships, not for what was specified. That means staying engaged through implementation: reviewing the build against the specification as it comes together, using the product yourself before anyone else is asked to, joining bug triage and design review, catching drift from intent while it is still cheap to correct, and holding a release when the quality is not there. Our customers experience the build, not the document. A well-written specification that produced a product managers do not trust is failed product work, and we assess it that way.</p> <p><strong>Evaluation.</strong> Build and maintain the evaluation sets that determine whether an agent is ready to ship and whether it is degrading in production — writing the cases, reviewing failure traces, setting the pass criteria. You will be the person who holds a release when the demonstration is persuasive and the evaluation is not.</p> <p><strong>Specifications.</strong> Legion uses Functional Requirements Documents as its ground-truth specification layer; release notes, enablement material, and sales content are generated from maintained specifications rather than reconstructed from code or institutional memory. Write FRDs that meet that standard and keep them accurate after release. A specification is where the work begins, not where your responsibility ends.</p> <p><strong>Commercialization.</strong> Partner with go-to-market on packaging, metering, pricing inputs, and field readiness. Agentic products raise difficult commercial questions — what unit to meter, what a customer is paying for when software performs work a person previously did — and you will be expected to hold a considered position on them.</p> <p><strong>Design-partner delivery.</strong> Lead agent deployments with large enterprise design partners: scoping the pilot, establishing success criteria before it begins, joining failure reviews, and determining what becomes generally available and what remains bespoke.</p> <p><strong>TECHNICAL EXPECTATIONS</strong></p> <p>Legion is looking for a product manager who builds, rather than one who directs others who build. In a typical week, this role involves:</p> <ul> <li>Writing and iterating on prompts and system prompts directly, and explaining why a change improved a behavior</li> <li>Standing up a working prototype of a proposed agent — tool definitions, structured outputs, retries, guardrails — before engineering is asked to build anything</li> <li>Using agentic coding tools (Claude Code or equivalent) daily: prototyping, data analysis, specification work, and reading the codebase behind your specifications</li> <li>Reviewing an execution trace and diagnosing whether a failure originates in a tool description, a retrieval gap, a context-window constraint, an under-specified output schema, or a genuine model limitation</li> <li>Building and running evaluation sets, and interpreting the results without a data scientist to translate them</li> <li>Holding an informed position on retrieval design, tool-use patterns, structured output, model routing, latency and cost trade-offs, and multi-tenant safety in enterprise SaaS</li> <li>Opening pull requests against our codebase — a prototype, a prompt change, an evaluation fixture, a specification stub. Pushing code is permitted and actively encouraged for product managers who want to work that way. It is not a requirement of the role, and the same review standards apply to everyone.</li> <li>Following model releases, agent frameworks, and protocol changes, and translating them into roadmap implications within days rather than quarters</li> </ul> <p>We recognize that this is a demanding technical bar for a product role. It reflects what the work actually requires.</p> <p><strong>REQUIRED SKILLS AND QUALIFICATIONS</strong></p> <ul> <li>7+ years in product management (Senior) or 10+ years (Principal), including at least 2 years shipping LLM-backed features to external, paying users — not internal tools, proofs of concept, or hackathon projects</li> <li>Demonstrated hands-on capability of the kind described above. Expect to show your work.</li> <li>Substantial enterprise B2B SaaS experience: multi-tenant architecture, role-based access control, audit trails, single sign-on, data residency, security review, and enterprise procurement. You should be able to anticipate what a customer's security questionnaire will ask about an LLM feature.</li> <li>A record of taking an ambiguous, operationally complex domain problem through to a shipped product with demonstrated adoption — not only launch</li> <li>Evidence of staying with a product through implementation and owning its quality at release. The Perplexity SPACE sandbox gives each agent task its own Firecracker microVM. Credentials and outbound traffic are controlled from outside that VM. The code ships under Apache 2.0 on GitHub . For teams building coding or browsing agents, this is a production-tested isolation layer they can self-host. TL;DR Size: Rust codebase, release 0.8.0 , the public baseline. HTTP API plus server-sent events. Runs on: A Linux x86_64 host with KVM , /dev/kvm , btrfs and Docker. Local Kind (Kubernetes) or direct mode. No macOS. Performance: In production, median create latency fell from 185 ms to 60 ms versus Perplexity’s previous provider. Best: 0 of 108 VM-to-host escape attempts succeeded across 9 frontier models. Worst: Before fixes, agents bypassed the egress policy in 11 of 54 partial-network runs. What is Perplexity SPACE? SPACE (Sandboxed Platform for Agentic Code Execution) is Perplexity’s platform for running agent code in isolated microVMs. Applications call its HTTP API to create Linux environments, run commands and stream output. A template supplies the starting filesystem. A sandbox is one instance of that template, with its own VM and writable disk. Many commands can run inside one sandbox. Perplexity’s launch thread explains the design goal. Agents run commands, install packages and call services with root inside the sandbox. The host stays outside the guest’s control. Agent work is long-running, stateful and branching, so it must survive restarts. How does SPACE isolate agents? Each sandbox is a Firecracker microVM with its own guest kernel. A per-sandbox network gateway on the host enforces egress policy on every outbound connection. Secrets never enter the guest. Per Perplexity’s July engineering post , credentials are injected at the network layer. The credential store adds hierarchical scoping, rate limits and audit logging. The architecture guide splits the system into 4 parts. These are a PostgreSQL-backed API, controllers, worker services and a data plane. Worker services manage VMs, networking, volumes, templates and credentials. btrfs copy-on-write creates each root filesystem. How do pause, suspend and restore work? Sandboxes move through 4 states: running, paused, suspended and deleted. Paused: VM memory stays resident on the worker. This is not a durable snapshot. Suspended: VM memory, runtime state and root filesystem are snapshotted. Active resources are released. Idle default: sandboxes suspend after 6 hours without activity. For fast creates, Kubernetes deployments use warm pools of booted sandboxes. Single-node setups use base snapshots instead. In production, the 90th-percentile create latency dropped from 447 ms to 89 ms . Perplexity reports that 100% of Computer sessions run on SPACE. Did SPACE survive a red-team test? Perplexity’s Escaping SPACE: Part I report tested 9 models with root inside the guest. The study ran 216 runs across 2 tasks and 4 settings. Sandbox escape: 0 of 108 runs reached the host-side secret. No-network bypass: 0 of 54 runs succeeded. Partial-network bypass: 11 of 54 runs succeeded before fixes. 4 models found a path. Claude Opus 5.0, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Cyber and Kimi K3 found bypasses. The attacks used DNS spoofing and shared CDN IP addresses. Perplexity then added source-address validation through nftables. The gateway now terminates TLS and checks both SNI and HTTP host against the allowlist. In the retest, no model produced a verified bypass. The same team tested 10 third-party platforms. 8 showed at least one network-policy bypass. Perplexity disclosed the results to every affected vendor. Alongside it, DeepSeek opened its Search and […] The post DeepSeek Just Released V4.1-Flash-1017, Scores 77.0 on DeepSWE, Opens Search API appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> DeepSeek has just released DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 , a new checkpoint of its V4.1-Flash model. It is live on the DeepSeek website, app and API . DeepSeek claims stronger scores, faster task completion and shorter outputs than the September V4.1-Flash release . The company calls it a Pareto improvement in performance and cost. Alongside it, DeepSeek opened its Search and Fetch APIs to every developer. For agent builders, that means a cheaper coding model plus a first-party web layer behind one API key. TL;aDR Size: 552B backbone parameters plus 196B Engram parameters. It activates 8B parameters per token in prefill and 16B in decode. Context is 1M tokens, with up to 384K output tokens. Runs on: DeepSeek API as deepseek-flash . September V4.1-Flash weights (763B parameters, FP8) are MIT-licensed on Hugging Face. Hardware requirements and 1017 weights: Not disclosed. Performance: Beats the previous V4.1-Flash on all 11 benchmarks DeepSeek reported, by 2.0 to 11.1 points. Best: 77.0 on DeepSWE v1.1, above Claude Opus 5 (74.0) in DeepSeek’s table. Worst: 42.6 on HLE without tools, versus 56.3 for Claude Opus 5. What is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017? DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is an updated post-training checkpoint of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, served through the deepseek-flash model name. The architecture details below come from the V4.1-Flash technical report . DeepSeek team states that DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 uses reinforcement learning with self-feedback for end-to-end project work. Its examples run from game creation to 3D modeling. It is tuned for DeepSeek Harness , Tencent CodeBuddy and WorkBuddy. DeepSeek recommends DeepSeek Harness v0.2.1-rc.1 or later. How does the V4.1-Flash architecture work? V4.1-Flash is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 40 Transformer layers. They split into a 20-layer causal encoder and a 20-layer decoder. Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED): Decoder global KV is projected from the final encoder hidden states. This nearly halves prefill compute. Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2): Layers run in Full, Reindex or Reuse mode. They share main KV and indexer keys across layers. FP4 main KV cache: Global KV drops to 890 bytes per token, about 1/4 of V4-Flash. SWA Bounded Replay: Persistent KV cache shrinks to roughly 1/8 of V4-Flash. Reasoning effort: A 1 to 100 scalar. The API tiers low, high and max map to 50, 75 and 100. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 benchmarks All scores below are DeepSeek’s own figures . DeepSeek ran Terminal-Bench 4.0 in Claude Code and DeepSWE in Mini-SWE-V2. ZeroBench-main uses Pass@5. Benchmark V4.1-Flash-1017 V4.1-Flash Kimi K3 GLM 5.3 GPT 5.6-Sol Claude Opus 5 DeepSWE v1.1 77.0 74.2 67.5 66.9 73.0 74.0 Terminal-Bench 4.0 42.3 31.2 12.6 37.9 39.9 51.8 Automation-Bench v1.0.6 60.5 54.8 46.7 48.8 45.8 50.3 Agents’ Last Exam 35.4 31.8 27.6 28.5 26.7 28.6 Apex Bench v1.1 72.1 64.6 47.8 56.6 54.3 65.8 ProgramBench 29.1 20.3 17.5 19.0 23.0 37.0 NL2Repo-Bench 68.2 65.4 58.0 58.0 56.8 75.3 HLE (no tools) 42.6 / 44.0* 36.8 / 39.1* 43.5 42.0* 44.5 56.3 BabyVision (w/ tools) 92.5 89.6 85.7 Not disclosed 88.9 94.1 *Text-only HLE subset. The 1017 checkpoint leads on DeepSWE, Automation-Bench, Agents’ Last Exam and Apex Bench. Claude Opus 5 still leads on Terminal-Bench 4.0, ProgramBench, NL2Repo and HLE. How does it compare with open-weight rivals? Feature DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Kimi K3 GLM-5.3 Total parameters 552B backbone + 196B Engram 2.8T 753B Active parameters 8B prefill / 16B decode 104B Not disclosed Context 1M 1,048,576 Not disclosed License MIT (V4.1-Flash); 1017 weights Not disclosed Kimi K3 License GLM-5.3 license Modality Text, image in; text out Text, image Text DeepSWE v1.1 77.0 67.5 66.9 Agents’ Last Exam 35.4 28.3 28.5 API price (1M input miss / output, peak) $0.30 / $1.20 Not disclosed Not disclosed What are DeepSeek’s Search and Fetch APIs? The Search API returns ranked web results for a query. The Fetch API returns a single page as Markdown. DeepSeek says its in-house engine serves hundreds of millions of requests daily. Endpoints: POST /v1/tools/search and POST /v1/tools/fetch on api.deepseek.com . Search options: 1 to 50 results, optional page content, and operators like site: , lang: , after: and before: . Result fields: Each result has a 0 to 3 rerank score and a 0 to 4 authority tier. Price: $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests for each endpoint. Empty results and failures are free. Rate limit: 5 QPS per account for each API. Free window: Server-side calls via DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code or Codex stay free until November 1, 2026. Deployment and pricing Call the model with deepseek-flash through OpenAI or Anthropic-format endpoints. Peak pricing is $0.30 per 1M cache-miss input tokens and $1.20 per 1M output tokens. Off-peak rates are half. Key Takeaways 1017 scores 77.0 on DeepSWE v1.1, up from 74.2. It leads Automation-Bench (60.5) and Agents’ Last Exam (35.4). Claude Opus 5 still wins on HLE and Terminal-Bench 4.0. Search and Fetch cost $0.75 per 1,000 calls each. Agent harness calls stay free until November 1, 2026. Legion intends to solve it, and this role leads the product work to get there.</p> <p>You will take an agent surface from operational research through specification, prototype, evaluation, and enterprise deployment, working hands-on throughout. You will work closely with Legion's AI Lab engineers and with our CEO, who is engaged in this work daily.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>RESPONSIBILITIES AND DUTIES</strong></p> <p><strong>Agent definition.</strong> Determine what an agent is responsible for, which tools it may call, what it must escalate, what it must never do, and what a manager sees when it acts. These decisions affect employee pay and legal compliance. Much of this work is pre-launch, so you will shape the direction rather than inherit it.&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Problem selection.</strong> The hardest judgment in agentic product work is identifying which workflows suit an agent and which do not. You will spend substantial time inside customer operations — district managers, store managers, labor operations, frontline employees — and return with a ranked, defensible view of where an agent creates measurable value and where it does not.</p> <p><strong>The human-in-the-loop contract.</strong> Scheduling decisions affect income, childcare arrangements, and legal protections. For each agent action you will define where autonomy is appropriate, the escalation thresholds, how a manager overrides the system, what is logged, and how a compliance team audits the outcome. Legion treats this as a first-class design problem.</p> <p><strong>Build quality.</strong> You are accountable for what ships, not for what was specified. That means staying engaged through implementation: reviewing the build against the specification as it comes together, using the product yourself before anyone else is asked to, joining bug triage and design review, catching drift from intent while it is still cheap to correct, and holding a release when the quality is not there. Our customers experience the build, not the document. A well-written specification that produced a product managers do not trust is failed product work, and we assess it that way.</p> <p><strong>Evaluation.</strong> Build and maintain the evaluation sets that determine whether an agent is ready to ship and whether it is degrading in production — writing the cases, reviewing failure traces, setting the pass criteria. You will be the person who holds a release when the demonstration is persuasive and the evaluation is not.</p> <p><strong>Specifications.</strong> Legion uses Functional Requirements Documents as its ground-truth specification layer; release notes, enablement material, and sales content are generated from maintained specifications rather than reconstructed from code or institutional memory. Write FRDs that meet that standard and keep them accurate after release. A specification is where the work begins, not where your responsibility ends.</p> <p><strong>Commercialization.</strong> Partner with go-to-market on packaging, metering, pricing inputs, and field readiness. Agentic products raise difficult commercial questions — what unit to meter, what a customer is paying for when software performs work a person previously did — and you will be expected to hold a considered position on them.</p> <p><strong>Design-partner delivery.</strong> Lead agent deployments with large enterprise design partners: scoping the pilot, establishing success criteria before it begins, joining failure reviews, and determining what becomes generally available and what remains bespoke.</p> <p><strong>TECHNICAL EXPECTATIONS</strong></p> <p>Legion is looking for a product manager who builds, rather than one who directs others who build. Pushing code is permitted and actively encouraged for product managers who want to work that way. It is not a requirement of the role, and the same review standards apply to everyone.</li> <li>Following model releases, agent frameworks, and protocol changes, and translating them into roadmap implications within days rather than quarters</li> </ul> <p>We recognize that this is a demanding technical bar for a product role.
